content: The human nervous system, or a psychological construct, raises questions about whether it is innate, learned, or a combination of both. This debate has been ongoing since Meyer’s observations in 1967. Many theorists, beginning in the third quarter of the 19th century, have posited that diatonic scales and tonality are derived from natural overtones. This perspective gained traction following the publication of Helmholtz's seminal work, On the Sensation of Tone, in 1862. Scholars such as Riemann, Schenker, and Hindemith have contributed extensively to this line of thought, emphasizing the natural basis of tonal systems. Rudolph Réti distinguishes between two types of tonality: harmonic tonality, which is characteristic of traditional homophonic music, and melodic tonality, which is found in monophonic music. He argues that in harmonic progressions like I-x-V-I, the V-I step is the only one that inherently produces the effect of tonality. All other chord progressions, whether diatonic or not, are the result of the composer’s creative invention. According to Réti, melodic tonality is fundamentally different from classical harmonic tonality. In melodic tonality, the entire melodic line is understood as a musical unit based on its relationship to a central note, which is not always the tonic as interpreted in harmonic tonality. Réti provides examples from ancient Jewish and Gregorian chant, as well as other Eastern musical traditions, to illustrate melodic tonality. He notes that these melodies can often be interrupted at any point and return to the tonic naturally. In contrast, harmonically tonal melodies, such as those in Mozart’s The Magic Flute, follow strict harmonic-rhythmic patterns. These patterns include points where deviation would be illogical and would disrupt the intrinsic sense of the melodic line. Réti observes that in harmonically tonal melodies, the tonic feels natural after each note, as seen in Mozart’s The Magic Flute. However, melodically tonal melodies resist harmonization and only reappear in Western music after the abandonment of harmonic tonality. This shift is exemplified in the works of Claude Debussy, where melodic tonality combined with modulation represents a modern approach to tonality.
